BORN INTO THE EXCLUSION OF THE OLD REGIME
Guelatao, 1806
Born to Zapotec parents
in a village of just twenty
families.
Orphaned at age three.
Raised working the fields,
speaking no Spanish, in a
town with absolutely no
schools.
The Systemic Lock
In early 1800s Oaxaca, a
poor indigenous youth had
exactly one path to an
education or a scientific
career: The Priesthood.
For those without wealth
to travel, the local
ecclesiastical system held
a complete monopoly on
social mobility.

THE ARCHITECTURE
OF INEQUALITY
The legacy of the colonial viceroyalty was not
just economic-it was legal. Society was
stratified by fueros (special jurisdictions). The
state was entirely subjugated to the whims of
the armed and the ordained.
The Military
& The Clergy
Protected by "fueros", these
classes existed outside and above
common civil law. They commanded
wealth, avoided civil courts, and
subverted the state.
The Civil State
& The People
Subject to extortionate parish
fees, forced labor, and an
impotent civil justice system.

THE WALK TO OAXACA
The Drive:
Driven by a vehement desire
to learn, Juárez rejected
agricultural destiny.
The Departure:
On December 17, 1818, at
twelve years old, he fled his
uncle's house on foot.
The Arrival:
He arrived in Oaxaca City that
night, finding work harvesting
cochineal for two reales a day,
and eventually securing a place
with a pious bookbinder,
Antonio Salanueva, who
supported his schooling.

CRUCIBLE I:
THE INJUSTICE AT
LOXICHA (1834)
As a young lawyer and legislator, Juárez
defended the indigenous people of Loxicha
against a corrupt priest who was extorting
them for parish fees and forced labor.
The Result:
Despite the evidence, the Church
colluded with the civil prefect. The
villagers were arrested. When Juárez
sought their release, a corrupt judge
falsely accused him of vagrancy and
inciting rebellion. Juárez was
imprisoned in the capital for nine days
without due process.

THE STOICISM OF LEADERSHIP
As Governor of Oaxaca, Juárez enforced laws banning burials inside churches for public health. In 1850, his two-year-old daughter,
Guadalupe, died. The law exempted the Governor's family, but Juárez refused the privilege. He carried his daughter's coffin to the
public cemetery outside the city walls himself, cementing the law through unimpeachable personal example.

THE ANATOMY OF A REVOLUTION: LEY JUÁREZ
Extinguishing Civil Fueros:
Stripped the Catholic Church of its
special civil courts, forcing clergy to
answer to common civil law.
Ley de
Administración
de lusticia
(Nov 23, 1855)
Restricting Military Power:
Confined military courts exclusively
to strictly military crimes, ending their
immunity from civilian justice.
The Declaration of War:
It was imperfect, but it served as the spark that ignited the ultimate reform.
It was a 'cartel of defiance' thrown at the privileged classes.

DISMANTLING THE MACHINERY OF POWER
WHAT WAS DISMANTLED
Disbanded the permanent standing
army (a constant threat to liberty and
source of mutinies)
Abolished the 'Commandancies General
which subverted state sovereignty to
military whims.
Eliminated theatrical military uniforms
and armed guards for the governor.
WHAT WAS ESTABLISHED
Organized a civilian National Guard.
Maintained peace solely through the
moral and legal authority of the civil
governor.
Wore the standard suit of a common
citizen, proving respectability comes
from the law, not theater.

THE ARCHITECT'S
LEGACY
Benito Juárez transformed a fractured, post-colonial
society ruled by military might and clerical privilege
into a modern Republic governed by civil law. Notes for
my children is not just a memoir; it is the ledger of a
man who suffered the iniustices of his era so that he
could systematically dismantle them.
"The supreme law of the republic must be the
inviolable and sacred respect for the rights
of men and of peoples." - Benito Juárez
